qs.q: Both Burkitt's lymphoma and infectious mononucleosis are caused by what virus?
qs.e: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is the causative agent of infectious mononucleosis and is strongly associated with the development of Burkitt's lymphoma, particularly in endemic regions.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Epstein‑Barr virus causes a self‑limited illness of adolescents with fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytosis. The disease is immune‑mediated, not directly cytopathic.

sections.p: Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that infects oropharyngeal epithelial cells and B lymphocytes. Primary infection in adolescents produces a classic self‑limited syndrome.
b: EBV is a double‑stranded DNA virus in the Herpesviridae family.
Primary infection usually occurs in late childhood in low‑resource settings, often asymptomatic.

sections.p: EBV is a large, enveloped virus with a linear DNA genome. It establishes lifelong latency in B cells.
b: Latency proteins LMP1 and EBNA‑2 drive B‑cell proliferation.

sections.p: Transmission is mainly via saliva; close contact or kissing spreads the virus. After epithelial entry, EBV infects B cells, leading to clonal expansion and a vigorous CD8+ T‑cell response.
b: Latent infection persists in memory B cells; reactivation is rare.

sections.p: Infectious mononucleosis presents with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytosis. Complications include splenic rupture and, rarely, hepatitis or encephalitis.
b: Immune‑mediated symptoms arise from cytotoxic T‑cell attack on infected B cells.

sections.p: Clinical suspicion is confirmed by heterophile antibody (Monospot) test or EBV‑specific serology. Atypical lymphocytes on peripheral smear support the diagnosis.
b: If tests are unavailable, rely on clinical picture and supportive care.

t.b: Detects heterophile antibodies; positive indicates EBV infection. A negative result does not exclude disease in early phase or in children.
IgM indicates recent infection; IgG seroconversion confirms exposure. Useful when Monospot is negative.
Shows atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells); helps differentiate from other causes of lymphocytosis.

sections.p: No antiviral therapy is routinely indicated. Management focuses on supportive care: rest, hydration, antipyretics, and avoidance of contact sports until splenomegaly resolves.
b: Avoid NSAIDs that increase bleeding risk in splenic enlargement.

sections.p: Remember that EBV causes a self‑limited disease; heterophile antibodies are the key diagnostic tool. Splenic rupture is a life‑threatening complication; advise patients to avoid contact sports for 4–6 weeks.
b: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in endemic areas.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain (possible splenic rupture), high‑grade fever >7 days, jaundice, confusion, or signs of severe dehydration.

faq.q: Can EBV be transmitted by sharing utensils?
faq.a: Yes, saliva is the main route; sharing utensils can spread the virus, especially in crowded settings.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for EBV?
faq.a: No licensed vaccine is available yet; prevention relies on hygiene and avoiding close contact during outbreaks.

faq.q: Why is the Monospot test negative in some cases?
faq.a: Early in infection or in young children the heterophile antibodies may not yet be produced; EBV‑specific serology is then required.
